passage:
Deepak, you look nervous about tomorrow, so let me tell you my story. I'm Chinmay. At twenty-five they made me team lead over Sunil, Farida and Bhaskar, my friends from the first day. The first feedback I ever gave was to Sunil. I was so afraid of hurting him that I said, “It's nearly perfect,” and the report went out with an error. The next month, panicking, I over-corrected. I sent Farida a long, sharp email about her mistake, copying everyone. She didn't speak to me for a week.

Then Sunil told me over tea, “We don't need you soft or harsh. Just straight.” So I started giving feedback in private, early, with one thing that was good and one thing to change. It felt awkward for months. It got easier.

qa.q: Who received the first feedback Chinmay ever gave?
qa.a: The first feedback Chinmay ever gave was to Sunil.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay say, “It's nearly perfect”?
qa.a: Chinmay was afraid of hurting Sunil, so softening the truth felt safer than being straight.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change after Sunil's words over tea?
qa.a: Chinmay began giving feedback in private and early, with one good thing and one thing to change.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt receiving a long, sharp email copied to everyone?
qa.a: Farida probably felt humiliated and angry, exposed in front of everyone, which fits the week of silence.

grounding: An elder recalls becoming team lead of former friends, being too soft and then too harsh with feedback before finding a steady, respectful tone.

passage:
The client deck was due in two hours and the shared printer had jammed. Anjali, three weeks into managing her old college friends, looked at Kalyani's slides and winced. The numbers on slide four were wrong. “It's fine,” Anjali said quickly, then, “Well, mostly fine.” Kalyani's smile faded. “What does that mean?”

Anjali's face went warm. She took a breath. “Slide four has last quarter's numbers. I should have said so right away. Can we fix it together? I'll read the numbers, you type.” Kalyani nodded, a little stiffly. Twenty minutes later the slide was right.

“Thanks for telling me straight,” Kalyani said quietly, “instead of saying fine.”

qa.q: What was wrong on slide four?
qa.a: Slide four had last quarter's numbers.

qa.q: Why did Anjali say “It's fine” first?
qa.a: Anjali felt awkward correcting a friend and reached for softness before finding a straight tone.

qa.q: What did Anjali suggest to fix the slide?
qa.a: Anjali suggested reading out the numbers while Kalyani typed.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have felt on first hearing “Well, mostly fine”?
qa.a: Kalyani probably felt worried and unsure what was wrong, as the fading smile suggests.

grounding: A young manager of former friends feels awkward giving feedback, is too soft at first and then finds a steady, respectful tone.
